title: Intelkin
summary: A tool that uses neuroscience to predict how the brain responds to a design before anyone sees it, catching churn risk before launch instead of after.
narrative: Every retention tool on the market today is reactive — it watches what customers do after a feature ships, then reacts once the churn has already happened. I built Intelkin to move that read earlier: it runs a design through Tribe V2, Meta's brain-response model, before any real customer sees it, and returns which cognitive regions are overloaded and where. I dogfooded it on our own Recollab investor demo and it caught three friction points our team had gone blind to after six weeks staring at the same screens — that's the actual argument for the tool, not just the pitch. I'm upfront about the trade-off: it's predicting a general research population's brain responses, not Recollab's specific users, so it's a fast pre-launch signal, not a replacement for testing with real people. It's still a two-piece prototype (a clickable UI shell plus a working terminal pipeline) — the model itself turned out to be the easy part; reading its brain-region output by hand is the real bottleneck, which is why automating that with Claude Vision is the next step, not the model.

title: Langchain Aggregator
summary: Rebuilt a single automated guess at vendor matching into a five-agent system with a person approving every step — 8x faster quote turnaround, zero unapproved outreach across a 5-building trial.
tagline: Redesigning quote sourcing with AI Agentic Systems
previewPrompt: Tell me about the Recollab Langchain aggregator project.
narrative: Recollab builds software for property managers running large condo buildings, and one gap was blocking a signed contract: when something broke — a leak, an HVAC failure — property managers had no fast way to get multiple vendor quotes in front of them, just phone calls to whoever they already knew. I shipped a first working version in n8n in a week to close the deal, but "nearby" was doing too much work — no distance cap, no license or trade check — and it ran for two days queuing outreach to vendors outside a building's service area before we caught it. Once real customers depended on it, I rebuilt it as a proper multi-agent system: an orchestrator, a vendor-matching agent that checks known trusted vendors first, a vendor-sourcing agent for when there isn't a match, an outreach agent, a quote-aggregation agent, and a follow-up agent — with a person approving every quote and every hire, no exceptions. It ran live across 5 buildings with zero unapproved outreach or hires. The lesson I carry forward: don't ship a matching rule without a specific, testable boundary.

title: Boardy
summary: An independent product teardown of Boardy: an opt-in, transcript-free signal after each meeting that turns one-time introductions into relationships that hold, measured by a new metric called Sustain Rate.
tagline: The 70% Problem: The AfterLife of Introductions
previewPrompt: Tell me about the Boardy project.
narrative: I started using Boardy to find a warm intro into a product role in Toronto, and partway through the call I began auditing it instead. I interviewed it the way I'd run discovery on any tool: how it picks matches, how often it follows up, where its numbers come from, who checks them. It turned out to be good at the spark and blind to what happens after an intro. It put its follow-up rate at roughly 20 to 30 percent, then told me by text that the number was said off the cuff and shouldn't be treated as data, so I used the correction as the finding instead of the number. My proposal is an opt-in signal after each meeting that shares back only a chemistry score and action items, never the transcript. It feeds nurture messaging and a metric I call Sustain Rate: the share of intros where both people re-engage within 30 days. This is independent product thinking built from a public conversation, not Boardy roadmap, and the page says so up front. Two cheap tests come before any automation: whether people opt in at all (under roughly 20 percent and the project stops), and whether hand-scored chemistry predicts which connections stay active. I dropped my LinkedIn verification idea because it violates their Terms of Service, and chose SEC Form D over Crunchbase for checking funding. The status is Concept: the spec is written, and the mockups and a second pass with Boardy are still ahead.

title: Operators on the Go
summary: A Micromart product concept for Golden Ventures: Price Nudges, an SMS recommendation that tells an apartment or residential operator when a store's price is out of step with similar stores nearby, with a one-reply way to fix it.
previewPrompt: Tell me about the Micromart Price Nudges project.
narrative: Micromart's dashboard reports what happened (sales, transactions, top products) but never tells an operator what to do next, and pricing is a single field buried in the Products page. I built a case study for Golden Ventures around Price Nudges: a text message that flags a price out of step with similar stores nearby and lets the operator fix it with one reply. I started with gyms as the instinct, then checked about 85 profiles in Micromart's Pro Operators directory: apartments and residential were named 24 times and offices 20, against 9 for gyms, so v0 targets apartment and residential operators, with gyms as a secondary example. I weighed four options (a dashboard panel, a dedicated operator app, SMS, and auto-applied prices) and chose SMS because it rides a channel operators already use and lands in a spare moment of their day, like a coffee line, and I ruled out auto-apply because it removes the human approval step. The north star is the share of active operators who make at least one pricing or promotion decision through Micromart in a month. The page includes two working prototypes, an SMS thread and a Price Nudges dashboard. The status is Concept, not shipped.
